# Trail Pheromone Deposition and Evaporation in Argentine Ants

## Positive Feedback in Path Selection

Foraging workers of the Argentine ant (*Linepithema humile*) establish collective transport networks between the nest and scattered nectar or protein sources. When a scout discovers a food source and returns to the nest, it deposits volatile trail pheromones from its Pavan's gland onto the substrate along the return trajectory. Subsequent outgoing workers detect the chemical gradient with their antennae and choose branches probabilistically in proportion to local pheromone concentration.

Because ants traveling along a shorter branch between the nest and food complete round trips faster than ants traversing a longer detour, the shorter branch receives fresh pheromone deposits at a higher rate per unit time. This autocatalytic positive feedback rapidly amplifies the relative attractiveness of the shorter path until nearly the entire foraging stream converges onto the minimum-length route.

## Role of Volatile Evaporation Against Stale Optima

Positive feedback alone would permanently lock the colony onto the first discovered path even after a food patch is exhausted or blocked by an obstacle. To prevent lock-in, trail pheromones undergo continuous first-order volatilization and degradation over time according to:

$$\frac{d\tau_{ij}(t)}{dt} = -\rho \, \tau_{ij}(t) + \sum_{k=1}^{m} \Delta \tau_{ij}^{k}(t)$$

Here $\tau_{ij}(t)$ is the pheromone concentration on trail segment $(i, j)$, $\rho \in (0, 1)$ is the evaporation decay constant, and $\Delta \tau_{ij}^{k}(t)$ is the pheromone deposited by ant $k$. When a food source depletes and returning ants stop laying fresh pheromone, exponential decay $-ho \, \tau_{ij}(t)$ erases the obsolete trail and allows exploration of alternative branches.

# Adaptive Packet Routing in Dynamic Telecommunication Networks

## Failure Modes of Static Shortest-Path Routing

Wide-area packet-switched telecommunication networks and multi-hop wireless backhaul meshes carry highly variable burst traffic across topologies subject to transient link congestion and fiber cuts. Conventional link-state routing protocols compute deterministic single-path shortest routes via periodic global topology flooding.

When traffic surges or links experience intermittent packet loss, static shortest-path routing tables oscillate or concentrate all flows onto congested bottleneck links until slow global routing convergence completes. During convergence transients, routers experience buffer overflow, elevated jitter, and routing loops that degrade voice and real-time control traffic.

## Requirements for Local Probabilistic Forwarding Tables

Network engineers seek decentralized routing schemes in which individual routers maintain probabilistic next-hop forwarding tables updated solely from lightweight probe packets traveling between source-destination pairs. When forward or backward probes measure lower end-to-end queuing delay along an alternative hop, the corresponding routing entry weight should be reinforced proportionally to path quality while older routing weights decay exponentially so obsolete paths are forgotten after topology changes.
